newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus leader meet to discuss union deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus leader meet to discuss union deal.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko met on Thursday to iron out differences over a controversial union deal, one day before its planned signing.

"When you leave, we'll take off our jackets and start working hard, checking article after article," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling reporters before the meeting. The two leaders are due to sign a union charter on Friday.

Despite a widely declared commitment by both leaders to move towards closer integration between the two Slav states, Yeltsin and the hardline Belarus president appear at odds over some key issues, including the ultimate aim of the union.
Lukashenko has made clear that Belarus would remain a sovereign state, rejecting talk that a closer alliance in the form of a federation could be formed.
"We have a certain limit -- our Soviet experience. Under the Soviet Union we (Belarus) had our own United Nations membership," Lukashenko said before he left Minsk.
Yeltsin said earlier this week that he saw Russia and Belarus merging into a single federative state by the end of the integration process, comments which prompted an angry reaction in Minsk.
Belarus negotiators are seeking a tight union between two independent states, each of which would have equal rights.

Lukashenko's nationalist opponents in Belarus have condemned the planned union as a plot by Moscow to revive the empire and rob Minsk of the independence it won when the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.
Russian liberals bitterly oppose the union, saying a deal with Lukashenko could hurt Russian democracy and tarnish Russia's image abroad.
But opinion polls show that the majority of the population in both states support the idea of close integration between the two former Soviet republics.
Lukashenko has said he hoped a personal meeting with Yeltsin could clear up remaining differences. But the Russian president clearly indicated that his capacity for compromise was not endless.

"We have agreed to meet with Lukashenko on May 22, so we do," Yeltsin said. "We will agree everything we need to agree without taking decisions which would contradict the interests of our countries and peoples."
